The angel of the LORD asks how long God will withhold mercy from Jerusalem after seventy years.
Jesus asks whether God will not give justice to his elect who cry to him day and night, and promises he will do so speedily.
Under the altar the souls of those slain for the word of God cry 'How long?' and are told to rest until the number of their fellow servants is complete.
The prayers of the saints rise with incense from the golden altar, and fire from the altar is thrown on the earth.
The altar itself answers, 'Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are your judgments.'

The cry 'How long?' is the classic lament of the faithful who suffer while God seems silent. Shed blood is pictured as having a voice that reaches God, and in the sacrificial system blood was poured at the altar's base, which makes the martyrs' position under the altar an image of their lives offered to God. Revelation shows the cry heard: the prayers rise before God, set the judgments in motion and are finally answered with praise for God's justice.

Laments asking how long a god would stay angry are known from Mesopotamian prayers, giving the biblical form a wider setting. 1 Enoch 47 describes the prayer and blood of the righteous rising before the Lord of Spirits until the number of the righteous is reached, and in 4 Ezra 4:35-37 the souls of the righteous in their chambers ask 'How long?' and are told to wait until the number like them is complete; later rabbinic texts place the souls of the righteous beneath the throne of glory. Romans prized noble deaths, and Christians in Asia faced the threat of execution, as Pliny's letter to Trajan later shows.

Revelation follows the 1 Enoch and 4 Ezra pattern closely, with a cry for vengeance answered by a waiting period until a number is complete, but places the souls under the heavenly altar. Where the Psalms ask God to avenge his servants among the nations, Revelation gives the martyrs white robes and rest first. The altar that hears their cry in 6:9 later speaks in 16:7 to affirm the justice of the bowl judgments.

Preterists often identify the martyrs with those killed under Jewish and Neronian persecution and the vindication with AD 70 or Rome's judgment, historicists with martyrs across church history, and futurists with believers killed in the end-time tribulation, sometimes with those of earlier ages. Idealists read the scene as the persistent prayer of the suffering church in every age, and Spiritual Understanding readers may stress the believer's present offering of life to God.
The marriage supper and the great supper of God
Isaiah's feast for all peoples and Ezekiel's grim banquet for the birds become two contrasting suppers in Revelation 19.
On Mount Zion the LORD prepares for all peoples a feast of rich food and aged wine, and swallows up death for ever.
After Gog's defeat God invites the birds and beasts to a sacrificial feast of the flesh of the mighty and the blood of princes.
Many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.
In the parable of the wedding feast the invited refuse, others are brought in, and a guest without a wedding garment is cast out.
A guest blesses those who will eat bread in the kingdom; Jesus answers with a great banquet the invited refuse and the poor and lame fill.
The angel says, 'Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.'
An angel standing in the sun calls the birds to 'the great supper of God' to eat the flesh of kings, captains and all people.

The meal is one of the Bible's richest images of salvation: God as host, his people welcomed, joy and plenty at his table. Jesus' table fellowship and parables present the kingdom as a banquet whose guest list surprises the righteous. Revelation sets two suppers side by side: the joyful wedding feast for those invited by the Lamb and the grim feast of judgment, in which the enemies of God become the meal.

Ancient Near Eastern texts celebrate a god's victory with a banquet, as when Baal holds a feast after building his palace in the Ugaritic texts. Second Temple writings speak of a messianic banquet: 1 Enoch 62:14 says the righteous will eat with that Son of Man, 2 Baruch 29:4 makes Behemoth and Leviathan food for the survivors, and the Qumran Rule of the Congregation (1QSa 2) describes a meal led by the priest and the Messiah of Israel. In the Greco-Roman world wedding feasts and banquets marked social rank, and leaving corpses unburied for birds was a grave dishonour.

Revelation 19 brings Isaiah's feast and Ezekiel's sacrificial meal together in the same chapter, so that the blessing and the curse are parallel invitations. Ezekiel's banquet follows Gog's defeat, while Revelation's precedes the defeat of the beast and his armies and includes 'all people, free and slave, small and great'. The parables' wedding feast becomes the marriage of the Lamb, with the bride clothed in the righteous deeds of the saints rather than a guest's garment.

Futurists usually place the marriage supper at or after Christ's return, with dispensationalists often locating the marriage in heaven before the return and the supper in the millennial kingdom, and the great supper at the battle of Armageddon. Preterists may connect the suppers with the new covenant feast and the judgment on Jerusalem or Rome, while idealists and amillennialists read them as the final consummation and judgment pictured in contrasting meals, with the Lord's Supper as a present foretaste, a theme Spiritual Understanding readers often stress.
The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David
Jacob's lion of Judah and Isaiah's shoot from Jesse become the conquering Messiah, who appears in Revelation as a slain Lamb.
Jacob calls Judah a lion's cub and promises that the sceptre will not depart from Judah until the one comes to whom the obedience of the peoples belongs.
A shoot will come out from the stump of Jesse and a branch grow from his roots, a new David from a cut-down royal line.
On that day the root of Jesse will stand as a signal for the peoples, and the nations will seek him.
The LORD will raise up for David a righteous Branch who will reign as king and do justice in the land.
Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 from the Greek version to show that the root of Jesse rises to rule the Gentiles, who hope in him.
An elder tells weeping John that the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered and can open the scroll.
Jesus names himself the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star, in the book's closing words.

The lion stands for the royal strength promised to Judah, and the root or shoot stands for a Davidic king who would rise again after the dynasty seemed finished. Together they name the expected Messiah who would rule Israel and draw the nations. Revelation keeps both titles but redefines the victory: the Lion who has conquered is seen as a Lamb standing as though slain, so the Messiah wins by sacrificial death.

The lion was a common royal symbol in the Ancient Near East, from Assyrian royal lion hunts to the lion-lined processional way of Babylon. Second Temple Jews read Genesis 49:10 messianically: a Qumran commentary on Genesis (4Q252) says the sceptre waits for the coming of the Messiah of righteousness, the Branch of David, and in 4 Ezra 11-12 a lion roaring from the forest is the Messiah who rebukes the eagle, usually taken as Rome. In the Roman world emperors claimed the right to rule the peoples, so a Jewish king of the nations was a rival claim.

Revelation 5:5-6 sets what John hears beside what he sees: he is told of a Lion and turns to see a Lamb, which reinterprets the militant hope rather than discarding it. Isaiah's root is a shoot growing from Jesse, but Revelation 22:16 calls Jesus both root and descendant of David, which many read as claiming he is both source and offspring of the line. Paul uses Isaiah 11:10 for the Gentile mission, while Revelation uses it within a heavenly enthronement scene.

All four schools identify the Lion and Root with Christ. Preterists, idealists and amillennial readers usually see Revelation 5 as Christ's enthronement after his resurrection and ascension, while many futurists place the scene in heaven before a future tribulation, and premillennial readers expect the Davidic reign to be fully realised on earth in the millennium.
The bright morning star
The star out of Jacob and the dawn of salvation become a title of Jesus and a promise to those who conquer.
Balaam sees a star coming out of Jacob and a sceptre rising out of Israel to crush Moab.
The king of Babylon is mocked as the Day Star, son of Dawn, fallen from heaven after trying to raise his throne above the stars of God.
For those who fear the LORD's name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings.
Zechariah sings that the dawn from on high will break upon us, giving light to those who sit in darkness.
The prophetic word is a lamp in a dark place until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.
To the one who conquers in Thyatira Christ promises to give the morning star, alongside authority over the nations.
Jesus calls himself the bright morning star, linking the title directly to his Davidic descent.

The morning star, the planet Venus as seen before sunrise, announces that night is ending and day is near. In Numbers the star is a coming ruler from Israel, and the prophets and Gospels speak of a dawning of salvation. Revelation applies the title to Jesus as the Davidic king whose rising signals the new day, and promises that his faithful people will share in it.

Venus as morning and evening star was linked with gods across the ancient world, such as Ishtar in Mesopotamia and Phosphoros or Lucifer, the light-bringer, in Greek and Latin. The Damascus Document (CD 7.18-21) and the Qumran Testimonia (4Q175) read the star of Numbers 24:17 as a messianic figure, and in AD 132 Simon ben Kosiba was hailed as Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star', on the strength of this verse. Roman imperial propaganda also used stars and dawn imagery for the emperor's divine favour and the deified Caesars.

Isaiah 14:12 uses the image for a proud king who falls, while Revelation 22:16 gives it to Jesus who rises, so the same picture can describe a usurper or the true king. Numbers' star is a conqueror over Moab; Revelation joins the star to the shepherding rule of Psalm 2 in 2:26-28. Second Peter places the rising of the morning star in believers' hearts, while Revelation presents the star as a gift that is ultimately Christ himself.

Most interpreters of every school take the promised morning star as Christ himself, or a share in his royal glory, given to the faithful. Futurist and historicist readers tend to stress its fulfilment at his return, preterists and idealists the present reign of the risen Christ, and Spiritual Understanding readers the dawning of Christ within the believer, as in 2 Peter 1:19.
Faithful witness, firstborn of the dead, ruler of the kings of the earth
Three titles from the royal Psalm 89 present Jesus as the true witness, the first to rise, and the king over all kings.
God promises to make David his firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.
David's throne will be established for ever like the moon, a faithful witness in the skies.
God made David a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples.
Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
Christ is the head of the body, the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might be pre-eminent in everything.
John greets the churches from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth.
To Laodicea Christ speaks as the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God's creation.

Psalm 89 gathers the promises to David: a firstborn son who stands above all kings and a throne as lasting as the moon, the faithful witness in the sky. Revelation applies all three ideas to Jesus, who bore true witness to God even to death, was the first to rise to the life of the age to come, and now holds authority over earthly rulers. The titles set the pattern for his followers, who are also called to be faithful witnesses, like Antipas in Revelation 2:13.

In the Ancient Near East the king was often called the son or firstborn of a god, and Psalm 89 uses that language for David. In Greek 'witness' is martys, and by the second century the word was already coming to mean a martyr, one who testifies by dying. In Roman Asia the emperor was honoured as ruler of the world and client kings depended on him, so calling a crucified Jew the ruler of the kings of the earth was a political as well as a religious claim. Laodicea lay close to Colossae, and Colossians 4:16 mentions a letter to the Laodiceans, so the echo of 'firstborn' and 'beginning' in 3:14 may reflect language already known there.

Psalm 89 is a lament that the Davidic promise seems broken, and Revelation answers it with a king whose throne is secure because he has passed through death. The psalm's faithful witness is the moon; in Revelation it is a person whose testimony cost his life. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits and firstborn of the dead to ground the coming resurrection of believers, and Revelation uses the title as a source of courage for those facing death.

The titles are not disputed between the schools, but the scope of 'ruler of the kings of the earth' is: preterists, postmillennialists and amillennial idealists stress Christ's present reign since the resurrection, while futurists and historic premillennialists often see it as rightful now but publicly enforced only at his return.
A kingdom of priests
Israel's calling at Sinai to be a priestly kingdom passes to the redeemed of every nation, who reign with Christ.
At Sinai God tells Israel that if they keep his covenant they will be to him a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
The restored people will be called priests of the LORD and ministers of God, and will enjoy the wealth of the nations.
The holy ones of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it for ever.
The kingdom and dominion under the whole heaven are given to the people of the holy ones of the Most High.
Believers are built as living stones into a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices.
Peter applies Exodus 19:6 to the churches: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation.
Christ, who freed us by his blood, has made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father.
The new song says the Lamb made people from every tribe and nation a kingdom and priests, and they shall reign on the earth.
Those who share in the first resurrection will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with him a thousand years.

To be a kingdom of priests is to belong wholly to God, to have access to him, and to stand between God and the nations as his representatives. Israel received this calling at Sinai, and the prophets looked for its renewal, while Daniel adds that the saints will share the kingdom itself. Revelation says the Lamb's death has created this priestly, ruling people out of every nation, and that they will reign.

Ancient Near Eastern kings often acted as chief priests, so joining royalty and priesthood was familiar, but Exodus extends it to a whole people. The Greek translation renders Exodus 19:6 as 'a royal priesthood' (basileion hierateuma), the form 1 Peter quotes, and Jubilees 16:18 and 33:20 echo the phrase for Israel; the Qumran community saw itself as a priestly holy house. In Roman Asia the high priests of the imperial cult were drawn from wealthy elites, while Revelation gives priesthood to ordinary believers, including the poor and the slave.

Exodus makes the calling conditional on keeping the covenant; Revelation grounds it in what Christ has already done through his blood. Revelation 1:6 and 5:10 follow the Hebrew 'a kingdom, priests' rather than the Greek 'royal priesthood' used by Peter. Daniel's saints receive the kingdom after the beasts are judged, and Revelation 5:10 and 20:6 likewise speak of reigning, which makes timing a key question.

Amillennial idealists and many preterists hold that believers already reign as priests now, with Revelation 20:6 describing the present reign of believers or of departed saints with Christ; postmillennialists stress the gospel's growing influence. Premillennial futurists and historic premillennialists take 'they shall reign on the earth' and the thousand years as a future reign after Christ's return, and some manuscripts' 'they reign' in 5:10 is part of the debate.
The key of David
The royal steward's key over David's house becomes Christ's authority to open and shut entry into God's kingdom.
Shebna, the steward over the royal house, is condemned for carving a grand tomb for himself and will be thrust from office.
God gives Eliakim Shebna's robe and the key of the house of David: what he opens no one will shut, and what he shuts no one will open.
Eliakim is fixed like a peg in a secure place, yet the peg will finally give way under the weight of his family.
Jesus gives Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, with authority to bind and loose.
The risen Christ says he was dead and is alive for ever, and holds the keys of Death and Hades.
To Philadelphia Christ speaks as the one who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut.
He sets before the small, faithful church an open door that no one is able to shut.

In Isaiah the key belongs to the steward who controlled access to the king and the royal household, so it means delegated authority to admit or exclude. Jesus gives keys of the kingdom to Peter, and in Revelation he holds the key himself, as the Davidic Messiah who decides who enters God's kingdom and who has power over death. For a weak church shut out by others, the promise is that the door Christ opens stays open.

The office 'over the house' is known from Hebrew seal impressions and from a tomb inscription at Silwan in Jerusalem that some scholars link to Shebna. Ancient keys could be large wooden or metal objects carried on the shoulder, as Isaiah 22:22 says. In Greek religion the goddess Hecate was described as holding the keys of Hades, and some scholars, including Aune, suggest Revelation 1:18 answers such claims. Philadelphia's letter mentions 'the synagogue of Satan' (3:9), which suggests that the Christians there had been excluded from the local Jewish community.

Isaiah's Eliakim is a human steward whose peg eventually gives way, but the one who holds the key in Revelation is 'the holy one, the true one', whose authority does not fail. Matthew's keys are given to an apostle for the church's ministry, while Revelation's key remains in Christ's hand. Revelation turns the language of exclusion around: those who seemed shut out are the ones before whom the door stands open.

Most readers see the key as Christ's messianic authority over entrance into the kingdom, and the open door as either access to the kingdom or an opportunity for mission. Some historicist and dispensational readers take Philadelphia as a picture of a later missionary era of church history, preterists tie the letter to conflict with the synagogue before AD 70, and idealists apply it to faithful churches in every age.
The Word of God
The creating, prophetic word of God becomes the name of the rider on the white horse who judges with a sword from his mouth.
God speaks, 'Let there be light', and there is light, so creation comes into being by his word.
By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth.
The word that goes out from God's mouth will not return empty but will accomplish what he purposes.
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory.
The word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, judging the thoughts of the heart.
John testifies to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, which make up the content of the book.
The rider on the white horse is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and his name is called the Word of God.

In the Hebrew Bible God's word is his effective speech: it creates, it commands, and it accomplishes his purpose. John's Gospel identifies that word with a person who became flesh, and Hebrews describes it as a sword that judges. Revelation uses 'the word of God' for the message the martyrs hold to, and then gives the same name to Christ as he comes to judge, so the one who conquers does so by the word that comes from his mouth (19:15).

Ancient Near Eastern texts sometimes speak of a god's word as a powerful force, and in Egyptian thought the god Ptah creates by speech. Greek philosophers, especially the Stoics, spoke of the Logos as the rational principle ordering the world, and the Jewish thinker Philo of Alexandria described the Logos as God's agent in creation. Aramaic Targums often use the 'Memra' or word of the LORD where the Hebrew speaks of God acting. The Wisdom of Solomon 18:15-16, a book in the Greek Old Testament, pictures God's all-powerful word leaping from the royal throne like a stern warrior with a sharp sword on the night of the Passover, a striking parallel to Revelation 19.

Genesis and the Psalms present the word as creating; Revelation 19 presents it as judging, with the sword coming from the mouth rather than held in the hand. John's Gospel speaks of the Word becoming flesh in humility, while Revelation shows the same Word coming in power. The robe 'dipped in blood' recalls the treader of the winepress in Isaiah 63:1-3, where the blood is the enemies', though many interpreters think Revelation means Christ's own blood, since he is already wearing it before the battle.

Futurists and most historicists see Revelation 19:11-16 as the visible second coming at the end of the age. Preterists often read it as Christ's judgment on his first-century enemies or the ongoing triumph of the gospel, and idealists as the victory of Christ through his word throughout history, completed at the end; the sword from the mouth leads many in all schools to stress that he conquers by speech rather than physical weapons.
The two witnesses, two olive trees and two lampstands
Two prophets with the powers of Moses and Elijah testify, are killed, and are raised, echoing Zechariah's olive trees and lampstand.
Moses strikes the Nile and its waters turn to blood, the first of the plagues on Egypt.
No one may be put to death on the evidence of a single witness.
Every charge must be established on the evidence of two or three witnesses.
Elijah announces that there will be neither dew nor rain except by his word, and the drought begins.
Zechariah sees a golden lampstand with seven lamps and two olive trees beside it.
The two olive trees are explained as the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.
God promises to send Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes.
Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus on the mountain of transfiguration, talking with him.
Two witnesses, called the two olive trees and two lampstands, prophesy 1,260 days, are killed by the beast, lie unburied, and are raised and taken up to heaven.

Two witnesses make testimony legally valid, so the number points to true and sufficient witness. Their powers to shut the sky and turn water to blood recall Elijah and Moses, the prophet and the lawgiver, while Zechariah's olive trees recall the anointed king and priest of the restored community. Their story follows Jesus' own: they bear witness, are killed in the great city, and are raised and vindicated before their enemies.

Zechariah's two anointed ones are usually taken as Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest. Jewish tradition expected the return of Elijah, and some texts expected Enoch as well, since neither had died; the Qumran community looked for a prophet like Moses and two messiahs of Aaron and Israel. Early Christian writers such as Hippolytus and Tertullian identified the two witnesses with Enoch and Elijah. Leaving bodies unburied was a grave insult in the ancient world, and the scene of the nations gazing and exchanging gifts parodies a public festival.

Zechariah has one lampstand and two olive trees; Revelation makes the witnesses both trees and lampstands, and in 1:20 lampstands are churches. Moses and Elijah each worked alone, but here the two share each other's powers. Unlike Elijah, who was taken up without dying, the witnesses die first and are then raised, following the pattern of the crucified and risen Christ.

Futurists usually expect two individual prophets in Jerusalem in the future tribulation, often Moses and Elijah or Enoch and Elijah. Preterists commonly see witnesses to Jerusalem before AD 70, sometimes the apostolic church, and historicists have read them as the two Testaments, the Law and the Prophets, or faithful witnesses such as the Waldensians through the 1,260 years. Idealists and many amillennial readers take them as the witnessing church as a whole, suffering and vindicated.
The woman clothed with the sun and her child
A woman in birth pains bears the ruling son whom the dragon seeks to devour, drawing on Eden, Joseph's dream and Zion in labour.
God sets enmity between the serpent and the woman's offspring, and tells the woman she will bear children in pain.
Joseph dreams that the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him, picturing Jacob's family.
God declares the king his son and gives him the nations, to rule them with a rod of iron.
Israel is like a woman writhing in labour who gives birth only to wind, unable to bring salvation.
Before her pains came, Zion gave birth to a son, so that a nation is born in one day.
Daughter Zion must writhe like a woman in labour and go to Babylon, yet there she will be rescued.
Paul says the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.
A great sign appears in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars, crying out in birth pains.
She bears a male child who is to rule the nations with a rod of iron; he is caught up to God, and she flees into the wilderness for 1,260 days.

The woman gathers up the people of God as mother: Eve whose offspring will crush the serpent, Israel with its twelve tribes, and Zion in labour giving birth to salvation. Her child is the Messiah of Psalm 2, and the dragon's attempt to devour him is the ancient serpent's war against the promised offspring. After the child is taken up, the woman is protected in the wilderness, as Israel was in the exodus.

Many scholars note a parallel with the Greek myth of Leto, pregnant with Apollo and pursued by the dragon Python, which was well known in Asia Minor and was used in imperial propaganda linking emperors with Apollo. Egyptian stories of Isis and Horus pursued by Set offer a similar pattern, and the goddess Roma was honoured across Asia as a queenly mother figure. In Jewish tradition the twelve stars recall the twelve tribes and the twelve signs of the zodiac, which Josephus and Philo linked with the high priest's twelve stones.

Joseph's dream has eleven stars, while Revelation's woman has twelve, a complete Israel. Isaiah's Zion gives birth without pain, while Revelation's woman cries out in labour, closer to Micah. Genesis promises a coming conflict between serpent and offspring; Revelation shows it reaching its decisive point, with the child taken up and the dragon thrown down.

Preterists often see the faithful Jewish community bearing the Messiah and the flight as the Jerusalem church's escape before AD 70; historicists commonly read the wilderness 1,260 days as the true church's long period of obscurity under persecution. Futurists usually identify the woman as Israel, protected in a future tribulation, and idealists as the people of God in both covenants. Roman Catholic readers also see a secondary reference to Mary, and Spiritual Understanding readers may read the birth as Christ formed within the believer.
Michael and the war in heaven
Daniel's angelic prince who stands for God's people leads the heavenly war in which the dragon, the accuser, is thrown down.
The angel tells Daniel that the prince of Persia resisted him until Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help.
No one contends on the angel's side against the princes of Persia and Greece except Michael, your prince.
At the time of the end Michael, the great prince who stands for your people, will arise in a time of unequalled trouble.
When the seventy return, Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.
As the cross approaches Jesus says, 'Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be driven out.'
The archangel Michael, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, does not presume to condemn him but says, 'The Lord rebuke you.'
War breaks out in heaven; Michael and his angels fight the dragon, who is thrown down to the earth with his angels.
A loud voice declares that the accuser has been thrown down, and that the believers conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and their testimony.

Michael is the angelic guardian of God's people, whose name means 'Who is like God?'. In Daniel he fights the spiritual princes behind earthly empires, and in Revelation he leads the war that throws Satan out of heaven. The hymn that follows explains the battle: Satan's role as accuser is ended by the blood of the Lamb, so the heavenly victory rests on the cross.

Ancient Near Eastern myth often told of a storm god defeating a sea dragon to win kingship, and Revelation 12 uses that pattern. In Second Temple Judaism Michael is named among the chief angels in 1 Enoch 20 and set over Israel, and the Qumran War Scroll (1QM 17) promises that God will raise the dominion of Michael among the angels. Early church writers say Jude 9 draws on a lost ending of the Testament or Assumption of Moses. The Satan as accuser in the heavenly court appears in Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3.
